content.value:
Dead wheels are much better than drive encoders, but they still have error.

Over a 120-inch path, drive encoders might be off by 6+ inches. Dead wheels might be off by half an inch — way better, but not zero.

Why? The pod can skip over tile seams, the omni wheel can slide sideways during fast strafes, encoder ticks are discrete, and the wheel diameter wears down over time.

If the starting pose you give the localizer doesn't match where the robot is physically placed, everything goes wrong.

Position error: you say (0, 0) but the robot is at (0.5, -0.3). Every waypoint in your path is now off by that amount.

Heading error: you say 0° but the robot is rotated 3°. Now every forward drive goes in the wrong direction. After 120 inches, that 3° error means you're over 6 inches off target — and it gets worse the farther you go.

content.question: You set the starting heading to 0° but the robot is actually at 2°. After driving 120 inches forward, how far off from the intended position will it be?
options: Not at all — heading error only matters when turning
About 4 inches — the heading error projects the drive into the wrong direction
The localizer automatically corrects for this

content.value:
Position drifts. Heading drifts too — and it's worse.

Pinpoint uses two dead wheel pods (forward + strafe) and gets heading from its built-in IMU. A three-pod setup without Pinpoint gets heading from the difference between the two forward pods — any encoder error in either pod becomes a heading error.

Either way, heading drift kills you because it projects your forward drive into the wrong direction, multiplying position error over distance.

Note: IMU heading also drifts over time. Gyroscope bias accumulates slowly, the magnetometer can be thrown off by metal near the robot, and vibrations from mechanisms like flywheels or launchers introduce noise into the gyro readings. It's better than pod-only heading, but not perfect.

content.question: Does an IMU heading drift over time?
options: No — IMU heading is always perfectly accurate
Yes — gyroscope bias accumulates and magnetometer can be affected by nearby metal
Only when the battery is low

content.value:
No single sensor is perfect. The solution is combining them:

Dead wheels → accurate distance, low slip. Handles position.

IMU → absolute heading reference. Slower to drift than pod-only heading.

AprilTags / vision → occasional absolute position fixes from field landmarks. Resets accumulated drift.
